1.pericope_label: Cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit

schools.summary: Note first that the verse belongs with the promises quoted at the end of the previous chapter and was cut from them by the chapter division. Then do the lexical work, because the word for filthiness settles the sense: it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, is used elsewhere of the pollution of idolatry and of the sin of Sodom, and its cognate verb of sexual impurity, so that idolatry and impurity were blended inextricably in the apostle's mind, and the Roman satirists show what defilement of the spirit could mean in that world. Give the other word its range as well -- a late term meaning to stain or pollute, taking in filthiness physical, moral, mental and ceremonial. Read the final clause as grammar rather than doctrine: the present tense makes this not the negative goodness of cleansing but something aggressive and progressive, a continuous process and not a sudden attainment; and note that Paul puts himself inside the exhortation rather than standing over it. Say plainly what the aim is -- perfect purity, entire holiness -- without pretending it is already reached.

Take the promises first and be exact about what kind of thing they are. God anticipates us by his pure favour, but having conferred it he requires gratitude in return, so that in every promise a condition is tacitly appended and the promises call us to sanctification as if God had interposed by an implied agreement. Hold that alongside the other Reformed reading, which insists these promises were held not in hope but in hand and in actual possession, and that being absolute and unconditional they are the clearest proof that a covenant of that kind breeds holiness rather than licence. Then define the two defilements by their evidence rather than their inwardness. If spirit meant the grace of regeneration the phrase about polluting the spirit would be absurd; so the demand reaches the visible man, and we are to be pure not only in defilements which God alone witnesses but in those that fall under the observation of others, consecrating the whole body and all its members. And press the polemical consequence: if inward superstition is defilement of the spirit, those who excuse outward idolatry on pretexts have left themselves nothing to call defilement of the flesh.

Join the verse to what precedes it, since the promises it rests on are in the last three verses of the previous chapter, and this is the second half of an exhortation begun earlier and resumed a few verses back. Then be concrete about the two defilements and do not blur them. The filthiness of the flesh means drunkenness, fornication, adultery and the sins done immediately against the body; the filthiness of the spirit means impure desires, unholy thoughts and polluting imaginations -- or, put at its shortest, all outward sin and all inward. Say where the remedy is to be sought: apply to God for the grace of purification, and avoid in spirit and practice everything opposed to his doctrine that tends to pollute the soul. And do not stop at the negative. Let us not rest in a negative religion, but carry holiness to its height in all its branches, enduring to the end in the loving fear of God, which is the sure foundation of all holiness.

Take the exhortation as a call to progress in holiness in both its branches, and name them. First, dying unto sin, the mortifying of our lusts and corruptions -- for sin is filthiness, there are defilements of body and mind alike, sins committed with the body and spiritual wickednesses, and we must cleanse ourselves from both, since God is to be glorified with body and soul. Second, living unto righteousness: if we hope God is our Father we must endeavour to partake of his holiness, to be holy as he is holy. Then set the standard where the text sets it and admit at once that it lies out of reach. We must be still perfecting holiness, not contenting ourselves with sincerity, which is our gospel perfection, but aiming at sinless perfection, though we shall always come short of it while we are in this world. And note that all of this is to be done in the fear of God, which is the root and principle of all religion, and that the promises themselves are the strong inducement to it.

debates.question: What kind of thing are the promises this exhortation rests on?

sides.position: Absolute and unconditional, and held not in hope but in hand and actual possession; which is clear proof that such a covenant breeds holiness rather than licence
Conditional by implication. God anticipates us by pure favour but then requires gratitude, so a condition is tacitly appended to every promise, as if God had interposed by an implied agreement

debates.question: What is filthiness of the spirit?

sides.position: Impure desires, unholy thoughts and polluting imaginations, as against the bodily sins of drunkenness and fornication
All inward sin, as the other is all outward
The contagion of the idol temple spreading to the inward parts; the noun is used elsewhere of the pollution of idolatry and of the sin of Sodom, and the Roman satirists show what it meant
Filthiness of every sort, physical, moral, mental and ceremonial
Inward superstition and impiety; from which it follows that those who excuse outward idolatry have nothing left to call defilement of the flesh

outliers.note: Alone reaches outside the Bible for evidence of what the phrase meant in that world, naming the Roman satirists as showing only too terribly what defilement of the spirit could be, and alone argues from the word's use elsewhere that idolatry and impurity were blended inextricably in the apostle's mind.

Alone sets the standard beyond reach and says so in the same breath, holding that we must not content ourselves with sincerity, which is our gospel perfection, but aim at sinless perfection, though we shall always come short of it while we are in this world.

themes: let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God

2.pericope_label: Receive us; we have wronged no man; I am filled with comfort

schools.summary: Read the request as being about doctrine as much as affection: do not let corrupt affections or unfavourable apprehensions keep this teaching from finding a place in you, since it would be unseemly for a man labouring with a father's zeal to be telling a story to the deaf. Then take the three denials as the standing faults of ministers, and name them as such -- an overbearing use of authority that breaks out into tyranny, the corrupting with false doctrine of those one ought to have guided, and an insatiable desire for what belongs to another. These are the things by which pastors commonly alienate their people. Admire next the restraint of the disclaimer that follows. The Corinthians deserved to be made the guilty party once Paul was acquitted, on two counts, ingratitude and calumny; yet he refrains from recrimination and stands simply on the defensive, since those who love do not assail but either cover a fault or soften it, a disposition to reproach being a sign of hatred. And mark the difference between condemning a man to blast him with infamy and condemning him to bring him back. Read the closing verse as a climax, boldness rising to glorying and glorying to a joy that dispels much grief.

Render the opening verb as make room for us, from the old word meaning to leave a space, and connect it to the complaint that they were straitened in their affections. Hear the pathos in it: having pleaded earlier about the contaminations of companionship with idolaters, he now entreats almost with sobs, as if to ask whether men who can find room for such as those have none for him. Take the denials as answers to specific charges -- whispers of greed and self-interested motives that he has to meet again later in the letter -- and render the second as ruining, which may cover money, morals or doctrine. On the disclaimer, note that there is no you in the Greek and that the vagueness looks intentional, leaving open whether he means his readers or others; here is a sudden revulsion of feeling as the recollection of good news rushes back. Trace the pledge to die and live together to a proverbial expression of strong attachment, with a profounder meaning behind it. And on the overflowing joy, note a compound verb found here alone in the New Testament, which is to have a regular flood.

Divide the three denials cleanly and let the divisions carry the sense: he had hurt no man in his person, corrupted none in his principles, defrauded none of his property. Note that in denying these he intimates the good he had done them, but with the utmost modesty, as though not looking at it. Then set the denial against the false teachers by name, since that is where it is aimed: they had beguiled the Corinthians from the simplicity of the truth, brought them into bondage, taken of them, devoured them and exalted themselves, and all of it had been patiently suffered. Take the disclaimer as tenderness rather than reproach -- not as if he accused them of laying anything to his charge -- and let the pledge to live and die with them stand as the strongest expression of affection, of the kind that makes a man prefer the beloved to all others; the poet's line about living and dying with a friend serves it exactly. Say honestly what the situation was: there was never a church less worthy of an apostle's affection at that moment, and never one more beloved.

Watch what the choice of words is doing. He does not say love us, but uses the phrase that appeals more strongly to their pity, make room for us; and he asks a favour that carries no burden and profits the giver more than the receiver. Having convicted them of being loved more than they loved, and of breaking away from his love to mix with pestilent men, he now softens the vehemence of his rebuke by asking for the very thing he reproached them for withholding, and so wins them to himself again. Add the reason this works: nothing so produces love as for the beloved to know that the one who loves him greatly desires his love. And notice what he leaves unsaid -- he does not recite the benefits he has conferred, but frames the speech another way, which is at once less offensive and more cutting, while alluding to the false apostles in the very denials he makes of himself.

debates.question: What is Paul asking for in the opening plea?

sides.position: Love, though he does not say love. He uses the phrase that appeals more strongly to pity, and asks a favour that carries no burden and profits the giver more than the receiver
Room in their hearts, the end of the tightness he had complained of, addressed even to the stubborn minority
A place for himself where they had found a place for men of evil lives; the entreaty is uttered almost with sobs
That they receive his doctrine as well as his person, not letting corrupt affections keep his teaching from finding a place in them

outliers.note: Alone explains why the plea takes the form it does, that Paul does not say love us but uses the phrase which appeals more strongly to pity, and alone observes that he refrains from reciting the benefits he had conferred, framing his speech in a way at once less offensive and more cutting.

Alone praises the restraint of the disclaimer, noting that the Corinthians deserved to be made the guilty party on two counts once Paul was acquitted, and that he refrains from recrimination because those who love do not assail but either cover a fault or soften it.

themes: Receive us; we have wronged no man, we have corrupted no man, we have defrauded no man
ye are in our hearts to die and live with you
I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation

5.pericope_label: No rest in Macedonia; God comforted us by the coming of Titus

schools.summary: Mark that the narrative has been resumed after a long digression, and mark the change of term with it: earlier he said he had no rest in his spirit, here that his flesh had no rest, so the body was still suffering want of rest even when the mind had begun to steady. Let the grammar show the disorder -- a dramatic perfect, a participle agreeing with neither case before it, a clause about fightings and fears standing as a parenthesis with no connecting particle. Do not overfix the fightings: they may be persecution from the heathen or conflict with the party of the circumcision, and we have no knowledge which; the fears manifestly concern the effect of the letter. Then treat the divine title as more than an epithet. Paul's own experience seems to present itself to him as an attribute of God's character, and the word for the cast down runs from low on the ground through low in condition to the abject -- perhaps with an allusion to a disparaging name others had used of him. Say last where the comfort really lay: not in the reunion but in the report, in their longing, their uttered lamentation, and a zeal exercised not toward Paul but on his behalf against those who slandered him.

Be exact about the limit Paul sets. In saying his flesh had no rest he means that as a man he had no relief, excepting the spiritual consolations by which he was meanwhile sustained; so he was afflicted in mind as well as body, and as a man knew nothing but great bitterness. Distinguish the two troubles by direction rather than by subject: the fightings are the outward assaults with which enemies molested him, the fears the anxiety he endured over the internal maladies of the Church, since it was public and not personal evils that disquieted him. Then draw the profitable doctrine from the divine title: God is wont to comfort those that are cast down, from which it follows that the more we have been afflicted the greater the consolation he has prepared, so that the epithet itself contains a choice promise for the miserable and those abased to the dust. Describe the persons meant as those humbled under his afflicting hand who have low apprehensions of themselves. And anticipate the obvious objection -- that a friend's arrival would naturally cheer anyone -- by answering that it was the condition of the Corinthians, not the presence of one man, that gave the joy.

Fix the itinerary before the exposition: from Ephesus to Troas, where he stopped some time, and then into Macedonia, from which this letter was written, so exceedingly anxious was he to know how the first epistle had sped. Take the flesh to mean simply ourselves. Then divide the trouble by its source, the fightings from without being the oppositions of pagans, Jews and false brethren, and the fears within concerning the brethren, lest they should be seduced. Break the anxiety into its parts, since that is what makes it real: lest the severity of the letter should alienate their affections, lest the party of the incestuous man should have prevailed, lest the false apostle's teaching should have perverted their minds. And then say the hard thing plainly -- that all was uncertainty and apprehension, and that the Spirit of God did not think proper to remove the causes of it in any extraordinary way. Name what Titus brought: their earnest desire to rectify what was amiss, their mourning because they had sinned, and the zeal they felt to testify their affection.

Trace the connection back to the earlier chapter, where he said he had no rest in his spirit at not finding Titus at Troas, and observe that his affection was such that in his further travels he still had no rest until he heard from them. Set out the distress in order: he was grieved at missing Titus because he could not learn how they had received him or how their affairs went; and besides that there were incessant storms of persecution, continual contentions with Jews and Gentiles without, and within a great concern for the new converts, lest they should be corrupted or seduced, and give scandal or take it. Then set out the comfort in the same order. The very coming of Titus was some comfort, it being matter of joy to see one long desired and expected; but the greater comfort was in what he brought.

sides.position: Paul's own anxiety about the effect of his letter
The same anxiety broken into parts: lest the severity should alienate them, lest the party of the incestuous man should prevail, lest the false apostle should have perverted them
Fears arising from the brethren, lest these should be seduced
Anxiety over the internal maladies of the Church, since it was public and not personal evils that disquieted him

outliers.note: Alone remarks that all was uncertainty and apprehension and that the Spirit of God did not think proper to remove the causes of it in any extraordinary way.

Alone makes the broken grammar carry the distress, noting the dramatic perfect, the participle agreeing with neither case before it, and the clause about fightings and fears standing as a parenthesis with no connecting particle.

themes: when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears
God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus
when he told us your earnest desire, your mourning, your fervent mind toward me

8.pericope_label: Though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent

schools.summary: Get the two verbs apart, because everything here turns on them. The word in the first verse means to be sorry again, to regret, and we have wrongly transferred its sense to the word that properly means a change of mind and life; that second word appears in the next verse in the fulness of its meaning. Note the imperfect in the concessive clause -- he was in a regretful mood at first -- and locate that moment either on first hearing of their grief or during his earlier anxiety, when he had half wished he had not written so strongly. Prefer regret to repent as the rendering, and note that the English variation between sorrowed and were made sorry answers to nothing in the Greek. Take the qualifying phrase literally as according to God, that is after his will and purpose. And guard the apostle where guarding is due: the word denotes only the uneasiness a good man feels from tenderness toward others and fear that what duty made him say might work too strongly, not any consciousness of having done wrong.

Explain why the letter was pitched as it was before defending its severity. The discourse was addressed to a whole church in which some thought ill of him and some well, some were doubtful and some confident, some docile and some obstinate; in consequence he had to direct his words now one way and then another to suit them all, so that he seems almost to sustain different characters. Then take away the offence of the severity on the ground of its outcome: their welfare was so much his object that he is delighted to see he has done them good. Add the caution that this softening is admissible only when the reproof has already done the good it was needed for. Say what he does not feel: no pleasure whatever in their sorrow, and had he the choice he would have promoted their welfare and their joy by the same means. There are physicians good and faithful in other respects who are nonetheless harsh and do not spare their patients; Paul is not of that disposition, and employs harsh cures only when necessity constrains him. Keep the feeling in view as well, that their grief as a natural passion gave him none, and so far as it pained them it pained him.

Attend to the exact form of the retraction, since the form is the argument. He does not say that he regretted before and does not regret now; he says that he does not regret, though he did. And the reason for putting it that way is not to confess that the rebuke overshot but to heighten their praise: the amendment they showed was so great that even supposing he had smitten them too severely and condemned himself for it, the result now vindicates the letter. Add the comparison that makes it plain -- little children who have undergone a painful remedy, an incision or a cautery or bitter physic, and are grateful afterwards. And note that he had made the same apology earlier, saying he wrote out of much affliction and anguish of heart, not that they should be made sorry but that they might know his love; here he establishes the same point at greater length, now that the sin has been corrected and tenderness carries no danger.

State the situation as experience rather than as theory: he had many doubts about how the letter would be received, and grieved at being obliged to write with such severity, the case absolutely requiring it; and he is not sorry now, because he finds it has completely answered the end for which it was sent. Then supply the practical test that keeps the doctrine honest -- a man may sorrow and yet not repent. What happened here was not sorrow at being found out and solemnly reprehended, but sorrow at having sinned against God, a consideration that weighed with them more than the apprehension of any punishment; and it produced a complete change of mind and conduct. Say too what the repentance spared them, since it is worth saying: it prevented that exercise of apostolic duty which would have consigned their bodies to destruction that their souls might be saved in the day of the Lord.

debates.question: Does the regret imply Paul had written too severely?

sides.position: No. The form of words heightens their praise rather than confessing excess: even supposing he had smitten too hard, the amendment justifies the letter
There was a moment when he half regretted having written so strongly, either on first hearing of their grief or in his earlier anxiety
No. The word denotes only the uneasiness a good man feels from tenderness toward others, not any consciousness of wrong
He grieved at being obliged to write so severely, the case absolutely requiring it, and is not sorry now because the letter answered its end

outliers.note: Alone reads the wording as praise rather than apology, observing that Paul does not say he regretted before and does not now but that he does not regret though he did, and that the point is to show how great the amendment was.

Alone explains the letter's pitch from the composition of its audience, that a church containing men favourable, hostile, doubtful, confident, docile and obstinate obliged the writer to turn his discourse now one way and then another, so that he seems almost to sustain different characters.

themes: though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent
now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance
that ye might receive damage by us in nothing

10.pericope_label: Godly sorrow worketh repentance; what carefulness it wrought in you

schools.summary: Settle what the verbal adjective attaches to, and be willing to disagree about it: one reading takes it with the salvation, another insists it agrees with the repentance and not the salvation, and it is found here alone in the New Testament. Either way the English effaces a distinction, and repentance unto salvation giving no matter for regret comes nearer. Note that this clause by itself should have prevented the confusion between mere sorrow and a change of mind and life. Define the sorrow by the phrase itself, as sorrow according with God's own view of sin, arising when our estimate of its evil and ill desert answers to his. Then describe its opposite exactly: the world's sorrow is grief for failure and not for sin, as in Cain, in Esau with his tears, and in Judas; and since it stands over against salvation, the death it works must be taken in the widest sense -- remorse and despair, the death of a broken heart, possibly suicide, in any case the loss of eternal life. On the marks that follow, number them and pair each with what it replaced: earnestness where there had been indifference or approval, the vindication sent through Titus, indignation at the offender, fear of the threatened chastisement and of God's judgment, longing for the apostle, new zeal for purity, and the sentence actually passed.

Define the sorrow by its author before its effects. It does not spring from free will, from natural conscience, from a work of the law or from fear of hell, but from free grace; it is a gift of the Spirit and the produce of almighty power, such as no means could effect of themselves, heightened by a discovery of God's love and views of pardoning mercy, and attended with faith. Define it also by contrast: worldly sorrow is despondency under earthly affliction, while this has an eye to God and reckons the one misery to be the loss of his favour. Make it the cause and origin of repentance, since a man who is not dissatisfied with himself, who does not detest his manner of life and grieve from an apprehension of sin, will never betake himself to the Lord. On the marks that follow, decline to argue whether they are effects of repentance or parts of it, since that is unnecessary for the design; the first of them means an eager and active assiduity in correcting what is amiss, set against the drowsiness that lies inactive while sin is unfelt. And be exact about the clearing: it consists rather in supplication for pardon than in extenuation of sin, as a son clearing himself to his father does not plead a case.

Say what the sorrow has for its object -- the breach of God's holy law -- and what it does, which is to work a thorough change of mind unto salvation, because the man who feels it cannot rest till he finds pardon through God's mercy. Then make the contrast concrete, since abstraction blunts it. Sorrow for lost goods, for lost friends, for the death of relatives, when it is poignant and deep, produces diseases, aggravates those already present, and often drives men to lay desperate hands on themselves; that sorrow leads to destruction and this to salvation, the one to heaven and the other to hell, and the death it works may be reckoned temporal, spiritual and eternal at once. On the seven marks, walk them through with the passages that explain each, and sort them by direction: apology and indignation with respect to themselves, fear and desire with respect to the apostle, zeal and revenge with respect to the offender -- the last being a kind of holy revenge taken upon themselves by men scarcely able to forgive themselves. And keep the final verdict exact: they were not clear of blame in the matter itself, only in their endeavours to remove the evil.

debates.question: What does the adjective giving no matter for regret qualify?

sides.position: Either repentance or salvation, and the latter seems preferable
It agrees with the repentance and not with the salvation

debates.question: How is godly sorrow distinguished from the sorrow of the world?

sides.position: By its author: not from free will, natural conscience, the law or fear of hell, but a gift of grace and the produce of almighty power
By its object: worldly sorrow is despondency under earthly affliction, while this reckons the one misery to be the loss of God's favour
By its measure: sorrow according with God's own view of sin, arising when our estimate of its evil answers to his
By its issue: grief for failure and not for sin, as in Cain, Esau and Judas, working out death in the end
By its ordinary effects: deep grief for lost goods or dead relatives breeds disease and drives men to lay desperate hands on themselves

outliers.note: Alone calls it a linguistic and theological tragedy that the English word repentance must serve for a term meaning change of mind and life, and insists that here the sorrow led to repentance and was not itself the repentance.

Alone corrects the sense of the clearing, holding that it consists rather in supplication for pardon than in extenuation of sin, as a son clearing himself to his father does not enter on a regular pleading of his cause.

themes: godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death
what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves
In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter

12.pericope_label: I wrote for the cause; we were comforted in your comfort

schools.summary: Identify the injured party and dismiss the alternatives: readings that make the apostle or the community the wronged man are fantastic, and the father is meant. Then press the difficulty rather than passing it, since the union was a marriage and could only have been one if the first had been dissolved by divorce, and a man who had divorced his own wife could hardly claim a wrong he had brought upon himself; the probable explanation is that the wife had divorced herself, a power wives held under Roman law and used with such licence that a satirist could speak of one who had eight husbands in five autumns. Note that the passage seems to show the father was still living when Paul wrote. On the following clause prefer the text that reads your earnest care for us rather than our care for you, the two pronouns being easily interchanged. Recover the structure of the next verse from its tense -- we have been comforted, and over and above our comfort we rejoiced the more at another's joy -- and note the doubled comparative as an ordinary idiom of the period.

Take the clause about their clearing themselves as the point of the verse: the Corinthians showed by plain evidence that they had no part in the crime with which their connivance had seemed to connect them. Then be careful how far the acquittal reaches. It palliates rather than clears them, since the undue forbearance they had exercised was not free from blame; and it acquits the body of the church rather than every member, for some had certainly countenanced the offence, though the disgrace fell upon all of them together. Note how he acts, as men do who desire a reconciliation: he wishes everything past to be buried, does not reproach or expostulate further, and forgets it all, being satisfied that they have repented. Then say what their comfort consisted in -- that having acknowledged the fault they did not merely take the reproof in good part but received it joyfully, since the bitterness of a reproof is sweetened as soon as its profit begins to be tasted. And draw the general rule for ministers, that the flourishing condition and well-being of churches yields them great pleasure and consolation.

Set out the candidates for the injured party before choosing, since the choice is not obvious: the apostle himself, the church, the offender's family, or his father. If the father is meant it would seem he was still alive, which makes the transgression more flagrant; though the words might equally be spoken of a dead man whose injured honour cried from the earth like Abel's blood. Then state the letter's real purpose plainly. It was not written to get the offender punished, nor merely to do justice to those who had suffered, but that they might have the fullest proof of the writer's fatherly affection for them and his concern for the honour of God -- not only, or chiefly, for the sake of the incestuous man or of his father, but to show his care over them. Add what follows from that: seeing it, they might see how unnatural their opposition to him had been. And note the plain evidence of the outcome, that their kind usage of the messenger was itself a full proof of their affection for the apostle.

Read these verses as consolation offered to people on whom the admonition has already worked. Say first that the former letter, severe as it might be thought, had a good design: it was not chiefly for the sake of the man who did the wrong, nor merely for the injured father and what satisfaction could be given him, but to manifest a sincere care for the whole church, lest it should suffer by letting such a crime and its scandal remain without due remark. Then let the joy be shared out as the text shares it. Titus was rejoiced and his spirit refreshed by their comfort, and that comforted and rejoiced the apostle also; and as Titus had been comforted while among them, so the remembrance of his reception among them renewed it afterwards.

debates.question: Who was the man that suffered wrong?

sides.position: The father, and the passage seems to show he was still living
The father; readings that make the apostle or the community the injured party are fantastic, and the wife must have divorced herself for the father to have been wronged at all
Four candidates are possible -- the apostle, the church, the family, the father -- and the words might be spoken of a dead father whose honour cried from the earth

debates.question: Whose care was the letter to make manifest?

sides.position: Paul's care for them, since discipline is administered with a view to the welfare of the whole body
Their earnest care for him. The correct text reads your care for us, the two pronouns being easily interchanged

outliers.note: Alone works out how the father could have been wronged at all, reasoning that the union was a marriage and so presupposed a divorce, and that the wife must have divorced herself, a power wives held under Roman law and used with such licence that a satirist could speak of one who had eight husbands in five autumns.

Alone prefers the reading your earnest care for us to our care for you, so that the clause states what the letter was to bring to light in the Corinthians rather than what it was to demonstrate in Paul.

themes: I wrote not for his cause that had done the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered wrong
that our care for you in the sight of God might appear unto you
we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus

14.pericope_label: Our boasting is found a truth; I have confidence in you

schools.summary: Supply the circumstance the verse assumes: the messenger had hesitated to go at all after an earlier mission failed, and was assured the Corinthians were sound at bottom and would come round if handled properly. Note the tense, which requires I was not shamed, and that the words I made are not in the Greek; note also the variant reading your boasting for ours, which would make the sense that what they said of themselves proved as true as what was said of them, though the received text gives the better sense -- we spoke truly to you of your faults and truly to Titus of your good qualities. Answer the apparent inconsistency: the same letter that boasted of them spoke plainly of their sins, and the two were not contradictory, as the outcome proved. On the word for inward affection, give the literal sense and say that heart or feelings serves best in English. Call the obedience of them all a remarkable statement of complete victory in spite of a stubborn minority still opposing the apostle. And correct the closing phrase, which does not mean I trust you but I am of good cheer, I take courage in you being what you are; with which he leaves a painful subject and turns, probably after a pause, to another.

Draw the character lesson from the boast, since that is what the verse shows: at the very time the Corinthians seemed unworthy of commendation he still promised much on their behalf, and reproving to their face those you love while hoping well of them and giving others good hopes of them is the signal evidence of a rightly constituted and candid mind. Such sincerity ought to have kept them from taking anything he said amiss. List what the boast had covered -- their faith in Christ, their liberality to the saints, their affection for him, their obedience as children to a father. On the word for inward affection, explain that the Greek names the viscera and came to stand for the seat of the emotions, so that it denotes compassion, love and every pious affection; and observe the purpose the report serves, that in describing the messenger as thus moved the apostle is working him into their affections, since it is an advantage that the servants of Christ should be loved. Then say what the closing verse is doing besides commending them: it paves the way for the request about the collection for the poor saints that follows.

Set the boast in time. The high character given of this church had been true before the false teacher got among them and changed their conduct and in great measure their character; now that they have returned to themselves and resumed the ground they lost, the old commendation is applicable again, and the boasting is found a truth. Then read the account of the messenger as a picture rather than a report: he is overjoyed even while delivering it, expatiating on it with delight, and he loved them for three reasons at once -- because they so loved the apostle, because they had shown kindness to himself, and because he found excellent gifts in them joined to humility. Take their receiving him with fear and trembling as reverence for his authority and dread lest anything he had delivered in God's name should be left undone. And say at the end what was at stake in the whole affair, that had the man who denied the resurrection and opposed the apostle's authority prevailed at Corinth, his influence might have spread over Greece and Asia Minor and destroyed the work of God there; which alone accounts for the depth of the anxiety this chapter records.

debates.question: How could the same letter boast of them and rebuke them?

sides.position: The two were not inconsistent, as the outcome proved; he had not hesitated to speak plainly of their sins in the very letter that assumed they were sound at bottom
They spoke truly to the Corinthians of their faults and truly to Titus of their good qualities; a variant reading would instead make it their own boasting that proved true
The high character had been true before the false teacher changed them, and became true again when they returned to themselves
It is the mark of a candid mind to reprove to the face those one loves while still hoping well of them and giving others good hopes of them

Alone corrects the closing phrase, holding that it does not mean I trust you but I am of good cheer, I take courage in you being what you are, and suggests that with this expression of thankfulness the apostle leaves a painful subject, probably after a pause, and turns to another.
